Takealot

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It’s a tale as old as online commerce itself: Where counterfeit products outdo the real thing by making cheaper replicas. But is the online platform, which professes its love for local businesses, s

Unique Selling Point:
3 strong case studies;
CASE STUDY 1: LifeVac anti-choking device
Ashley Enslin is a preschool teacher in Sumerset West, Cape Town who bought the product and it turns out to be fake. She lives in Summerset West and bought the product in March. We can do the interview at her preschool.
Nicolette Grace with the LifeVac anti-choking device: They are in Bedfordview, 30 Selwyn rd, Bedfordview. He has the actual fake device as well as the proper one. We can interview him at his warehouse if we want. He can show is the two versions : real and fake of the product.
CASE STUDY 2: PSN Protein
Paige Mullins is now heavily pregnant now – she says the sooner we interview her the better because she might go into labour next week. She lives in KZN. So we would just send a camera man. But I’ll be online and conduct interview with her, because she needs to explain the video she took of the actual product. We will recreate her ordering the product from Takealot. Then we will have her typing angry emails to Takealot and have her recreate her frustrations and show her taking the product. She lives at: Simbithi eco estate in Ballito, 4 bridelia close
Lauren is afraid to speak without her identity being hidden, and I think we can use her to speak as a case study who has been bullied by Takealot. She would prefer we don’t name the product and I think that’s not a problem. She’s taken quite a knock. She would highlight 3 big issues: the issue of how they treat sellers – because Paige complained and wrote a bad review, Takealot removed Lauren for 5 days online. They also forced her to sell her product at a lower price, and she hasn’t made a profit in 6 months. She lives in Sumerset West Cape Town.
CASE STUDY 3: Rapid Lash
Wayne Le Grange is the CEO of Blue Sky International that sells cosmetics mostly. We can set them up like they are doing a sting… we can have him ordering the fake product, and sending it out for testing to confirm is a fake. We can recreate him getting the product opening it and realizing it’s a fraud. He is in Cape Town: Stikland. ATRAX Logistics is our warehouse. Wed is fine. 28b Montreal Dr, Airport City, Cape Town, 7490.


Summary:
You’re ready to treat yourself to something nice online. You hit that "buy now" button, but when your package arrives, it isn’t what you ordered. And on top of that, turns out it's a cheaper, inferior product… a counterfeit or a fake product.
That is what is happening at Takealot.com. This has been an issue that consumers have been complaining about over the years on various websites.
We have three strong case studies:
Naspers owned…
CASE STUDY 1: While enjoying a party with her friends, Sally witnesses a child choking and is relieved when someone uses an anti-choking device to save the day. Eager to ensure their own safety, Sally and her friends turn to takealot.com to purchase the same life-saving device. However, their excitement quickly turns sour when they receive a counterfeit product after paying R1800. Disheartened, they reach out to the seller, Blake from Ventira, who imports the product from LifeVac. Despite Blake's efforts to alert Takealot, no action is taken. Fearing the impact of negative reviews on his product, Blake replaces the counterfeit devices for the ladies. He even has the fake products on hand to prove the deception. He has since then had to fight with Takealot to ensure they don’t provide a cheaper counterfeit product instead of theirs.
CASE STUDY 2: Paige Mullins and her mother, Colleen, craving some extra protein during Paige's pregnancy, opt for their favourite: PSN Protein by PSN Lifestyle. However, upon receiving their orders, they notice an odd taste and texture, prompting them to contact PSN Lifestyle's Lauren. To their dismay, Lauren confirms their suspicion: they've been duped by counterfeit versions of the product, likely orchestrated by copycats. Examination of the containers reveals subtle differences, with the genuine PSN product boasting superior quality and a distinctive shine. Frustrated, Paige complains to Takealot, only to face retaliation as they remove PSN Lifestyle's page from their platform. Takealot pressures Lauren to have Paige retract her negative review, resorting to bullying tactics over the following months. Despite the strain, Lauren continues supplying her product to Takealot at a loss to protect her brand. Paige's discovery exposes Takealot's deceit; their claim of the product being from the same manufacturer but a different seller proves false, as PSN Protein is exclusively manufactured by Lauren.
Turns out Paige discovers a whole host of other products that are having the same problem Lauren’s is: My Beauty Luv, Phoera Cosmetics, baby bottles, breast tape, Dear Deer and Rapid Lash.
CASE STUDY 3: Rapid Lash: Wayne le Grange CEO of Blue Sky International: Says they had this problem with Takealot since 2017. Despite their complaints being ignored, they conducted their own investigation in January 2024, ordering Rapid Lash and receiving a counterfeit product (see pictures). Taking action, they filed a charge of counterfeit goods at the Strand Police station against Takealot, with legal support from IP attorneys Adams & Adams. Alleging that Takealot profited from selling counterfeit goods (they take a percentage from all sales), they demanded product removal, which initially met resistance. Only after threats of legal action did Takealot comply.

Further information:
How they treat their sellers: if we hide her identity: Lauren's experience sheds light on the challenging dynamics between sellers and Takealot. Despite complaints about counterfeit products affecting her business, Takealot's response was punitive, with her product being removed for days. To salvage her brand's reputation, Lauren endured selling at a loss on Takealot for over six months. Moreover, Takealot's demands, such as storing her product in their warehouse, came with additional financial burdens and underscored her dependency on the platform. This highlights the power dynamics and challenges faced by sellers reliant on Takealot's platform for business success.

Instead of speaking to a consumer protection or IP lawyer we could speak to Wendy Knowler. She has specifically dealt with Takealot Renowned consumer advocate Wendy Knowler sheds light on Takealot's poor customer service, citing examples of selling stolen goods and price gouging. She says Takealot has 27,000 reviews on Hello Peter nearly 19,000 are 1 star.


Extra Budget Items:
If takealot don't speak, then we can pivot story around confronting a counterfeit product maker : the counterfeit supplier's details from Takealot themselves: Abigail Wade, located in Johannesburg (18 Rye Lane, Magaliessig, 065 982 1291, abigailwade@hotmail.co.uk, School of Aesthetics). Confrontation may be on the horizon…

Script:


VO1: South Africans are expected to spend R225 billion shopping online next year. It’s a highly competitive, 24/7 marketplace in which pricing is key.

LINK 1 - outside takealot: Picture it, you’re excited to buy yourself something nice online so you put the item in the cart, you hit the buy now button, and you wait, but when your package arrives, it’s not what you ordered. Even worse… it’s something cheaper and inferior.
VO2: As a mother to a young child, Amy Moses was anxious about choking hazards. Wanting to be prepared, she went online.
NEW SOUNDUP: as you know choking is one two three very quick um I ended up seeing this life Vac.
VO3: LifeVac, is a patented anti-choking device that has featured in dramatic viral videos like this one.
SOUNDUP: Video of the device saving child that was up front…. VO4: A policeman in the U.S. uses the device to clear the obstruction… a life saved.
CASE STUDY: Amy: I found it on Takealot and from lifevac. It was not in my budget but at least I did a payment plan.

VO5: But the product arrived without labeling or instructions. It also didn't have what’s known as a CE mark confirming the product has undergone health and quality checks.

Amy: So the packaging looked like I would say like a party packet like texture. It was quite easily bendable, the plastic for the mask, it's not supposed to be that, like bendable.
VO6: Amy thought she had ordered the genuine LifeVac but what she’d received was a cheaper knock-off.

Govan: Would you be comfortable using it on your own children?
Amy: No, not the fake version


LINK: It’s a tale as old as online commerce itself: Knockoffs tend to outsell originals, because they’re cheaper, but in this case, is the online platform, Takealot, which professes its love for local businesses, failing to safeguard the brands?

VO7: Takealot.com was profitable for the first time this year. Launched in 2011, it’s grown to 12,000 sellers with 90 pickup points nationwide.

Turning a profit in a tough economic environment is welcome news for the business. Less welcome are signs that its customers don’t always get what they pay for.

VO 8: The LifeVac device is imported EXCLUSIVELY into South Africa by a Johannesburg-based medical device company called Ventria.

UPS of Govan and Nicolette discussing the lifevac: Govan: This one has LifeVac on it, this one doesn’t. (FIND DIFFERENT BITE)

VO 9: Nicolette Grace is a director.

UPS: Nicolette: We started looking on Takealot seeing there are other products that are imitating the LifeVac - same branding, same content. About every second day we’re getting a complaint.

VO10: Takealot deals with thousands of products. Many of them are identical, imported and sold by different sellers, at slightly different prices. Takealot calls these “parallel products” and groups them into what it calls a buy box.

Let’s show you what we mean with this video from Ventria’s Takealot profile. Clicking on the seller link takes us to all the products sold by Ventria, including this space blanket. But when we select the space blanket, Takealot’s algorithm automatically chooses a slightly cheaper version. Note that the seller is different, but the photos and description of the product are Ventria’s. These two products are in the same buy box, but there’s no guarantee they are the same quality.
Nicolette: We've never heard of the lifevac device failing.
Govan: You don't know how the fake is performing?
Nicolette: No we don't.
VO11: It’s a problem impacting other sellers, too. (PAUSE) We spoke to more than 10 companies offering anything from cosmetics to baby bottles. All confirmed having customers who hadn’t received the brand they’d meant to order.

Another example: hair scrunchies from one local brand. Both are called Dear Deer, the pictures and description are identical, but Dear Deer sells them at R149: R9 more than the buy box offer from a different seller.

UPSOUND FROM VIDEO: Dear Deer, stone white and black, you place your order for stone white and black however this product looks nothing like the product you’ve ordered. It’s different colours. This is what the product should look like.
VO12: Takealot declined an interview, but in a written response said the products competing against the LifeVac are not "fake" or "counterfeit," but instead are a competing offer under a different "brand" name. Takealot strongly denied suggestions they aren't responsible for product safety.
On the scrunchies, Takealot says the similar listing has been removed.
Takealot says the buy box is designed to present the customer with the best product offer, whether on price or delivery time, and that it doesn’t limit the customer’s choice of brand.
But sellers feel differently.
Nicolette: When the consumer goes onto the buy box on to Takealot they'll actually think they purchasing a lifevac.

Govan: Takealot says it's a parallel product, you disagree?
Nicolette: I disagree.
LifeVac Global confirmed that there is no parallel because Ventria is the only importer.
VO13: Debates about parallel imports are one thing, but Takealot’s system may be allowing the sale of counterfeits.

UPS PAIGE: I've been eating the protein supplement for about 3 years 00:01:24,160 the protein supplement is the best tasting protein I have come across

UPS: PAIGE MAKING SUPPLEMENT

VO14: Earlier this year, vegetarian Paige Mullins, expecting her first child, ordered a trusted protein supplement on Takealot. But what she received was not the product she knew.

Paige: The quality wasn't good, there was like a residue left over at the end and the taste, some of them were salty, some of them were so sweet.

VO15: Paige contacted the manufacturer, who confirmed she’d been sent an imitation: The branding was copied and doesn’t have the same embossed labeling, and more importantly, the protein powder itself isn’t the original product.

Paige: Takealot flat out denied selling counterfeit products um even though it was very clear.

VO16: Paige recorded this screen video showing how a product from a different seller ended up in her cart, despite choosing the genuine brand.

ups: Paige: This was an order where i was sure to select the genuine seller, you can see that the seller has changed to this random seller, but if i click on the product, it takes me to the genuine supplier.
VO17: The buy box strikes again - but this time the “parallel product” is an imitation of the original.
Takealot says it’s not selling a counterfeit protein product, but instead had two sellers who both have intellectual property rights to the brand. Ultimately, Takealot removed the competing seller whose product Paige received.
For businessman Wayne Le Grange, the competition on Takealot posed an entirely different challenge - notably because there shouldn’t have been any. His company has the exclusive license to sell a product called Rapid Lash in Africa and they have an agreement with Takealot that no sales of the product would be allowed on their platform.

[PUT AD HERE - avoid showing pink box]

VO 19: It’s a hair loss treatment product sold only by licensed professionals. But Wayne has repeatedly found fake versions offered on Takealot.

UPS: Rapid Lash, Wayne le Grange: If you shake… that’s a viscous fluid.

VO 20: In March, Wayne bought the product masquerading as RapidLash on Takealot and sent it to company headquarters in California. Tests confirmed it was counterfeit: the liquid inside is more water than anything else.

UPSOUND GOVAN: This is water, this is already making me scared.

VO21: Wayne laid criminal charges against Takealot.

Wayne: Because takealot takes commission for every sale
Govan: Takealot profited?
Wayne: Yeah. profit yeah so they have to take responsibility they can't just say it's not us.
VO22: Takealot says it hasn’t confirmed the criminal charges as police haven't contacted it and it hasn’t located a sample of the alleged counterfeit.
LINK: Takealot states it has a strict zero-tolerance policy for counterfeit goods. And on the rare occasion that they are sold, it terminates the seller's account, it refunds the buyer, it recalls the product, and takes legal action.

VO: So are these cases a small minority, a consequence of the system Takealot uses to simplify the millions of sales it facilitates every day?

The sellers we spoke to say no. In June, Wayne again found a knockoff of his product on Takealot.
Wayne: This is the third time. how can they say they don't know?
Takealot insists its vetting process is robust, and that the buybox gives a better deal for THE SAME product. But we’ve seen that the products in the buybox are NOT the same or even equivalent. In fact, the buy box sometimes sets up a genuine brand against a counterfeit of its own product.
VO: A fake scrunchie isn’t going to do any harm, but other counterfeits have potentially more serious consequences.
UPS: Paige: It was scary to realize that I had been eating something I don't know what chemicals it contains…
INtv with Rapid Lash: Govan: I'll tell you right now I don't know what this is
Wayne: And I definitely wouldn't put the fake one anywhere near your eye
Govan: No
And knock-offs certainty have no place in matters of life and death.
Show video of lifevac videos.
Wayne: So it will destroy my company, destroy the families that work for me, will destroy this the clinics that work for us, we've estimated about 160,000 people's lives will be affected by this.

It was quite easily bendable, the plastic for the mask, it's not supposed to be that, like bendable. VO6: Amy thought she had ordered the genuine LifeVac but what she’d received was a cheaper knock-off. Govan: Would you be comfortable using it on your own children? Amy: No, not the fake version LINK: It’s a tale as old as online commerce itself: Knockoffs tend to outsell originals, because they’re cheaper, but in this case, is the online platform, Takealot, which professes its love for local businesses, failing to safeguard the brands? VO7: Takealot.com was profitable for the first time this year. Launched in 2011, it’s grown to 12,000 sellers with 90 pickup points nationwide. Turning a profit in a tough economic environment is welcome news for the business. Less welcome are signs that its customers don’t always get what they pay for. VO 8: The LifeVac device is imported EXCLUSIVELY into South Africa by a Johannesburg-based medical device company called Ventria. UPS of Govan and Nicolette discussing the lifevac: Govan: This one has LifeVac on it, this one doesn’t. (FIND DIFFERENT BITE) VO 9: Nicolette Grace is a director. UPS: Nicolette: We started looking on Takealot seeing there are other products that are imitating the LifeVac - same branding, same content. About every second day we’re getting a complaint. VO10: Takealot deals with thousands of products. Many of them are identical, imported and sold by different sellers, at slightly different prices. Takealot calls these “parallel products” and groups them into what it calls a buy box. Let’s show you what we mean with this video from Ventria’s Takealot profile. Clicking on the seller link takes us to all the products sold by Ventria, including this space blanket. But when we select the space blanket, Takealot’s algorithm automatically chooses a slightly cheaper version. Note that the seller is different, but the photos and description of the product are Ventria’s. These two products are in the same buy box, but there’s no guarantee they are the same quality. Nicolette: We've never heard of the lifevac device failing. Govan: You don't know how the fake is performing? Nicolette: No we don't. VO11: It’s a problem impacting other sellers, too. (PAUSE) We spoke to more than 10 companies offering anything from cosmetics to baby bottles. All confirmed having customers who hadn’t received the brand they’d meant to order. Another example: hair scrunchies from one local brand. Both are called Dear Deer, the pictures and description are identical, but Dear Deer sells them at R149: R9 more than the buy box offer from a different seller. UPSOUND FROM VIDEO: Dear Deer, stone white and black, you place your order for stone white and black however this product looks nothing like the product you’ve ordered. It’s different colours. This is what the product should look like. VO12: Takealot declined an interview, but in a written response said the products competing against the LifeVac are not "fake" or "counterfeit," but instead are a competing offer under a different "brand" name. Takealot strongly denied suggestions they aren't responsible for product safety. On the scrunchies, Takealot says the similar listing has been removed. Takealot says the buy box is designed to present the customer with the best product offer, whether on price or delivery time, and that it doesn’t limit the customer’s choice of brand. But sellers feel differently. Nicolette: When the consumer goes onto the buy box on to Takealot they'll actually think they purchasing a lifevac. Govan: Takealot says it's a parallel product, you disagree? Nicolette: I disagree. LifeVac Global confirmed that there is no parallel because Ventria is the only importer. VO13: Debates about parallel imports are one thing, but Takealot’s system may be allowing the sale of counterfeits. UPS PAIGE: I've been eating the protein supplement for about 3 years 00:01:24,160 the protein supplement is the best tasting protein I have come across UPS: PAIGE MAKING SUPPLEMENT VO14: Earlier this year, vegetarian Paige Mullins, expecting her first child, ordered a trusted protein supplement on Takealot. But what she received was not the product she knew. Paige: The quality wasn't good, there was like a residue left over at the end and the taste, some of them were salty, some of them were so sweet. VO15: Paige contacted the manufacturer, who confirmed she’d been sent an imitation: The branding was copied and doesn’t have the same embossed labeling, and more importantly, the protein powder itself isn’t the original product. Paige: Takealot flat out denied selling counterfeit products um even though it was very clear. VO16: Paige recorded this screen video showing how a product from a different seller ended up in her cart, despite choosing the genuine brand. ups: Paige: This was an order where i was sure to select the genuine seller, you can see that the seller has changed to this random seller, but if i click on the product, it takes me to the genuine supplier. VO17: The buy box strikes again - but this time the “parallel product” is an imitation of the original. Takealot says it’s not selling a counterfeit protein product, but instead had two sellers who both have intellectual property rights to the brand. Ultimately, Takealot removed the competing seller whose product Paige received. For businessman Wayne Le Grange, the competition on Takealot posed an entirely different challenge - notably because there shouldn’t have been any. His company has the exclusive license to sell a product called Rapid Lash in Africa and they have an agreement with Takealot that no sales of the product would be allowed on their platform. [PUT AD HERE - avoid showing pink box] VO 19: It’s a hair loss treatment product sold only by licensed professionals. But Wayne has repeatedly found fake versions offered on Takealot. UPS: Rapid Lash, Wayne le Grange: If you shake… that’s a viscous fluid. VO 20: In March, Wayne bought the product masquerading as RapidLash on Takealot and sent it to company headquarters in California. Tests confirmed it was counterfeit: the liquid inside is more water than anything else. UPSOUND GOVAN: This is water, this is already making me scared. VO21: Wayne laid criminal charges against Takealot. Wayne: Because takealot takes commission for every sale Govan: Takealot profited? Wayne: Yeah. profit yeah so they have to take responsibility they can't just say it's not us. VO22: Takealot says it hasn’t confirmed the criminal charges as police haven't contacted it and it hasn’t located a sample of the alleged counterfeit. LINK: Takealot states it has a strict zero-tolerance policy for counterfeit goods. And on the rare occasion that they are sold, it terminates the seller's account, it refunds the buyer, it recalls the product, and takes legal action. VO: So are these cases a small minority, a consequence of the system Takealot uses to simplify the millions of sales it facilitates every day? The sellers we spoke to say no. In June, Wayne again found a knockoff of his product on Takealot. Wayne: This is the third time. how can they say they don't know? Takealot insists its vetting process is robust, and that the buybox gives a better deal for THE SAME product. But we’ve seen that the products in the buybox are NOT the same or even equivalent. In fact, the buy box sometimes sets up a genuine brand against a counterfeit of its own product. VO: A fake scrunchie isn’t going to do any harm, but other counterfeits have potentially more serious consequences. UPS: Paige: It was scary to realize that I had been eating something I don't know what chemicals it contains… INtv with Rapid Lash: Govan: I'll tell you right now I don't know what this is Wayne: And I definitely wouldn't put the fake one anywhere near your eye Govan: No And knock-offs certainty have no place in matters of life and death. Show video of lifevac videos. Wayne: So it will destroy my company, destroy the families that work for me, will destroy this the clinics that work for us, we've estimated about 160,000 people's lives will be affected by this.

metadata.Summary: You’re ready to treat yourself to something nice online. You hit that "buy now" button, but when your package arrives, it isn’t what you ordered. And on top of that, turns out it's a cheaper, inferior product… a counterfeit or a fake product. That is what is happening at Takealot.com. This has been an issue that consumers have been complaining about over the years on various websites. We have three strong case studies: Naspers owned… CASE STUDY 1: While enjoying a party with her friends, Sally witnesses a child choking and is relieved when someone uses an anti-choking device to save the day. Eager to ensure their own safety, Sally and her friends turn to takealot.com to purchase the same life-saving device. However, their excitement quickly turns sour when they receive a counterfeit product after paying R1800. Disheartened, they reach out to the seller, Blake from Ventira, who imports the product from LifeVac. Despite Blake's efforts to alert Takealot, no action is taken. Fearing the impact of negative reviews on his product, Blake replaces the counterfeit devices for the ladies. He even has the fake products on hand to prove the deception. He has since then had to fight with Takealot to ensure they don’t provide a cheaper counterfeit product instead of theirs. CASE STUDY 2: Paige Mullins and her mother, Colleen, craving some extra protein during Paige's pregnancy, opt for their favourite: PSN Protein by PSN Lifestyle. However, upon receiving their orders, they notice an odd taste and texture, prompting them to contact PSN Lifestyle's Lauren. To their dismay, Lauren confirms their suspicion: they've been duped by counterfeit versions of the product, likely orchestrated by copycats. Examination of the containers reveals subtle differences, with the genuine PSN product boasting superior quality and a distinctive shine. Frustrated, Paige complains to Takealot, only to face retaliation as they remove PSN Lifestyle's page from their platform. Takealot pressures Lauren to have Paige retract her negative review, resorting to bullying tactics over the following months. Despite the strain, Lauren continues supplying her product to Takealot at a loss to protect her brand. Paige's discovery exposes Takealot's deceit; their claim of the product being from the same manufacturer but a different seller proves false, as PSN Protein is exclusively manufactured by Lauren. Turns out Paige discovers a whole host of other products that are having the same problem Lauren’s is: My Beauty Luv, Phoera Cosmetics, baby bottles, breast tape, Dear Deer and Rapid Lash. CASE STUDY 3: Rapid Lash: Wayne le Grange CEO of Blue Sky International: Says they had this problem with Takealot since 2017. Despite their complaints being ignored, they conducted their own investigation in January 2024, ordering Rapid Lash and receiving a counterfeit product (see pictures). Taking action, they filed a charge of counterfeit goods at the Strand Police station against Takealot, with legal support from IP attorneys Adams & Adams. Alleging that Takealot profited from selling counterfeit goods (they take a percentage from all sales), they demanded product removal, which initially met resistance. Only after threats of legal action did Takealot comply.
metadata.Further information: How they treat their sellers: if we hide her identity: Lauren's experience sheds light on the challenging dynamics between sellers and Takealot. Despite complaints about counterfeit products affecting her business, Takealot's response was punitive, with her product being removed for days. To salvage her brand's reputation, Lauren endured selling at a loss on Takealot for over six months. Moreover, Takealot's demands, such as storing her product in their warehouse, came with additional financial burdens and underscored her dependency on the platform. This highlights the power dynamics and challenges faced by sellers reliant on Takealot's platform for business success. Instead of speaking to a consumer protection or IP lawyer we could speak to Wendy Knowler. She has specifically dealt with Takealot Renowned consumer advocate Wendy Knowler sheds light on Takealot's poor customer service, citing examples of selling stolen goods and price gouging. She says Takealot has 27,000 reviews on Hello Peter nearly 19,000 are 1 star.
